mentions.text:
Just some notes from $TSLA transcripts:

Elon Musk: "I think Optimus will be the biggest product ever" from Q2 earnings transcripts.

Even from Q1, Elon Stated: "I think Optimus will be our biggest product. Not just Tesla's biggest product ever, but probably the biggest product ever.

And I remain convinced of that conclusion". 

It's very rare to see such high conviction reiterated from Elon regarding humanoids both directionally and TAM-wise.

In terms of upstream suppliers opportunities, Karn Budhiraj, VP of $TSLA supply chains stated: 

"We’re seeing the same level of investment going to memory and also new specific items like metal injection molded parts, flexible printed circuits, and all sorts of nonlinear technologies..." 

And that they had to build new supply chains from scratch. So would be interesting to look at for new supply chain supplier opportunities apart from the known ones.  

Just pulled older slides and it looks like capacity targets for Fremont are 1M and Giga Texas was 10M, so at scale, $TSLA seems to be the clear US leader. If you're looking at that S-Curve opportunity ramp. 

On a side note, Elon also gave a shoutout to $MU with likely reasonably priced LTAs, given his statement: 

"We really appreciate Micron making room for Tesla in the years to come and giving us actually a very significant allocation on reasonable terms given the pretty insane pricing of memory these days." (Just for structural memory demand).  

Elon also gave a shoutout to Panasonic which had invested many billions in increasing battery cell production (will need to do deeper DD into Panasonic after this), then Samsung and $TSM. 

Just takeaways from Tesla earnings TLDR: 

Elon tends to be directionally correct on where the future is heading, such as with EV or Space. 

He seems extremely bullish on humanoids.

mentions.text:
Per Truist, AI data center capacity goes from 24 GW to 100 GW by 2030, and every one of those watts has to be converted, stored, smoothed and cooled before a single GPU turns on.

So I mapped every business that gets paid between the grid and the chip, seven layers from the grid to the GPU, and marked the one I'd watch most closely.

Infrastructure // getting megawatts into the building:
$ETN Eaton, $VRT Vertiv, $GEV GE Vernova, $SBGSY Schneider, $ABBNY ABB

Power supply // AC in, DC out:
Delta (https://t.co/tAcP8vyGJW), the cleanest pure play on the whole map Lite-On (https://t.co/RZNOwxTpNN), co-designed the GB300 power shelf $FLEX Flex, $AEIS Advanced Energy

DC-DC conversion // the last step before the silicon, and THE LAYER I'D WATCH:
$MPWR Monolithic Power, $VICR Vicor, $IFNNY Infineon, $TXN Texas Instruments, $ADI Analog Devices, $RNECY Renesas, $ON onsemi
As density rises, every point of efficiency here is worth more, and that's where pricing power can show up.

Battery backup // seconds to minutes when power drops:
$PCRFY Panasonic, Samsung SDI (006400.KS), LG Energy Solution (373220.KS) 

Capacitors // fractions of a second when GPU demand spikes:
Nippon Chemi-Con (6997.T), $MRAAY Murata, $TTDKY TDK, Yageo (https://t.co/yXXDTFGgaV), Samsung Electro-Mechanics (009150.KS)

Control // the nervous system:
$NXPI NXP, $STM STMicro, plus TI, ADI and Infineon again

Cooling // where every watt ends up:
$VRT Vertiv, Delta, $NJDCY Nidec

Panasonic shows up in six boxes on the map and Delta in four, and to me that's the tell, because the names that keep popping up are the ones getting paid more than once every time a rack gets built.

I broke down all seven layers in my latest article on Substack, including why they grow on three different demand curves and the five holes in the thesis, because I don't do one-sided. 

It's free to read, link in the comments.

Bullish ⚡️
